description_full: The Cheesecake Factory Incorporated operates and licenses restaurants in the United States and Canada. It operates bakeries that produce cheesecakes and other baked products for its restaurants, international licensees, third-party bakery customers, external foodservice operators, retailers, and distributors. The company operates restaurants under the brands comprising The Cheesecake Factory, North Italia, Flower Child, and Fox Restaurant Concepts. The Cheesecake Factory Incorporated was founded in 1972 and is headquartered in Calabasas, California.
ceo_bio: Mr. David M. Overton | Founder, Chairman & CEO | Age 79 | Compensation: $2.5M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 48K people. Revenue per employee of $78K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $3K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $567 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 32× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: The Cheesecake Factory Incorpor is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.3B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 10% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $155M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.03× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 22× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 7.4% of the shares.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.60x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 135% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $154.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 64% in the 2020 crash, 38% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $64.10 (margin of safety -67%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 20%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $38.24 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 25.3 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 19.5 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 34.3 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 120% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $106 on average, in line with the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.7%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.04).
It converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.03x.
ROE of 34% is amplified by 7.5x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($215.7M of cash against $630.1M of debt), with interest covered 21.6x.
The current ratio of 0.59 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.6% over 3 years, 13.6% over 5 years and 6.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 55% of profits supports about 8.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 3.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 8.4% on average.
own: Insiders own 7.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (16 sales, net $25.5M sold).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (2.9% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 11.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 39.9% of the float, 7.8 days to cover.
people: With about 48,000 employees, each generates about $78K of revenue, 0.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 5.6% a year.
That works out to $3K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $2.5M (32x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
